conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that arthroscopy does not provide a meaningful or lasting improvement in pain or function for knee osteoarthritis compared to non-surgical care or placebo surgery, citing high-quality evidence and a strong recommendation against its use.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** For typical knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopy (including joint washout/lavage, debridement, and arthroscopic treatment of degenerative meniscal tears) does **not** provide a meaningful, lasting improvement in pain or function compared with non-surgical care or placebo surgery. It also entails recovery burden and surgical risks.

High-quality evidence supports this: a placebo-controlled randomized trial found lavage or debridement no better than placebo, and a later randomized trial tested arthroscopy plus optimized medical/physical therapy against optimized therapy alone. A 2022 Cochrane review concluded that arthroscopy offers little or no clinically important benefit for pain or function, likely no important quality-of-life benefit, and may not improve treatment success versus placebo.

Accordingly, the BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel makes a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopy for nearly all people with degenerative knee disease, including those with imaging-confirmed osteoarthritis or reported mechanical symptoms. This does not address unusual situations such as a genuinely locked knee from an acute mechanical obstruction; those require individualized orthopedic assessment.

For osteoarthritis symptoms, discuss evidence-based non-operative options—exercise/physical therapy, weight management if relevant, and appropriate pain management—with your clinician.

Sources:  
- https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease  
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259  
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333  
- https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982
